meta.title: Respiratory Protection
meta.description: Covers respiratory hazards, respirator types, medical evaluations, fit testing, seal checks, maintenance, and the written respiratory protection program requirements under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.134.

respiratory-hazards-basics.title: Respiratory Hazards in the Workplace
respiratory-hazards-basics.content: Workers can be exposed to a wide range of respiratory hazards including dusts, fumes, mists, vapors, gases, smoke, and oxygen deficiency. The body's natural defenses cannot protect against all airborne contaminants. Some hazardous substances can be inhaled without immediately obvious symptoms, yet cause serious long-term damage. Recognizing respiratory hazards is the first step in protecting workers.

engineering-controls-respirators.title: Engineering Controls Before Respirators
engineering-controls-respirators.content: When feasible, engineering controls such as ventilation systems, enclosures, and process changes should be used to reduce airborne contaminants before relying on respirators. Respirators are used as a last line of defense when engineering and administrative controls are not sufficient to reduce exposure to safe levels. OSHA requires employers to implement a hierarchy of controls.

respirator-types.title: Types of Respirators
respirator-types.content: Air-purifying respirators (APRs) remove contaminants from ambient air using filters, cartridges, or canisters. They cannot be used in oxygen-deficient atmospheres. Atmosphere-supplying respirators, including SCBAs (self-contained breathing apparatus) and supplied-air respirators, deliver clean air from an independent source. SCBAs are required in immediately dangerous to life or health (IDLH) atmospheres. Filter designations: 'N' (not resistant to oil), 'R' (resistant to oil), 'P' (oil-proof); efficiency: 95, 99, or 100 (HEPA).

fit-testing-seal-check.title: Fit Testing and User Seal Check
fit-testing-seal-check.content: A fit test must be performed before a worker wears a tight-fitting respirator for the first time and annually thereafter. Fit testing determines whether the respirator properly seals to the individual wearer's face. A user seal check must be performed every time the respirator is put on. Conditions that can interfere with a proper seal include facial hair in the sealing area, a damaged facepiece, and eyeglass temples under a full-face respirator.

maintenance-storage.title: Respirator Maintenance and Storage
maintenance-storage.content: Respirators must be inspected before each use and during cleaning. Defective parts must be replaced. Shared respirators must be cleaned and disinfected before use by another employee. Respirators should be stored in a clean, sanitary location away from contaminants, sunlight, and extreme temperatures. Damaged respirators must be removed from service and replaced.

written-program.title: Written Respiratory Protection Program
written-program.content: Employers with workers who wear respirators must develop and implement a written respiratory protection program. The program must include respirator selection procedures, medical evaluation procedures, fit testing procedures, training on the use and limitations of respirators, and procedures for cleaning, inspection, storage, and repair. A program administrator must be designated.

worker-responsibilities-respiratory.title: Worker Responsibilities Under the Program
worker-responsibilities-respiratory.content: Employees must use assigned respirators in accordance with their training and manufacturer instructions. They must perform seal checks every time they put on the respirator. If a respirator becomes damaged during use, the employee must leave the hazardous area safely and report the problem. Workers must never share an uncleaned respirator. If a worker feels dizzy, short of breath, or experiences irritation while wearing a respirator, they must exit the area safely and report the condition.

options.text: Every time the respirator is put on

Eyeglass temples under a full-face respirator seal

Remove it while still in the hazardous area

1.questionText: Which federal regulation establishes OSHA's requirements for respiratory protection in general industry?

2.questionText: A worker grinds metal, creating airborne dust and fumes. What type of workplace hazard is present?

options.text: A respiratory hazard from airborne particulates and fumes

3.questionText: True or False: The respiratory system can fully protect itself from all airborne workplace contaminants without the use of respiratory PPE.

4.questionText: What is the preferred method for reducing worker exposure to airborne contaminants before using respirators?

options.text: Use engineering controls like local exhaust ventilation
Reduce the number of workers in the area
Issue disposable dust masks to all workers

5.questionText: Before a worker can be assigned a respirator, what three things must occur?

options.text: Supervisor approval, tool checkout, and a site tour
Medical evaluation, proper respirator selection, and training
Annual review, background check, and a written test
Shift assignment, locker access, and PPE fit review

6.questionText: A worker must enter an atmosphere immediately dangerous to life or health. Which respirator provides its own independent air supply?

options.text: Full-face air-purifying respirator with organic vapor cartridge

7.questionText: True or False: An air-purifying respirator is safe to use in an atmosphere where the oxygen level is below normal.

8.questionText: An annual fit test is required for tight-fitting respirators. What does this test verify?

options.text: That the respirator meets color-coding requirements
That the respirator facepiece seals properly to each individual wearer's face
That the cartridges are not expired
That the worker has read the respirator instruction manual

9.questionText: A worker prepares to enter a confined space and dons a tight-fitting respirator. When should they perform the user seal check?

options.text: Each time the respirator is put on, before entering the hazard area
Once per week at the start of the work week
Only on the first day of a new work assignment
Only after completing fit testing for the year

10.questionText: Which of the following would most likely prevent a respirator from forming a proper face seal?

options.text: Facial hair, a damaged facepiece, or glasses under the seal

11.questionText: While working in a hazardous area, a worker's respirator strap breaks. What is the correct action?

options.text: Hold the respirator in place manually and finish the task
Remove the respirator inside the hazardous atmosphere
Leave the hazardous area safely and report the damaged respirator
Ask a coworker for their respirator

12.questionText: True or False: A respirator used by one employee can be issued directly to another employee without cleaning first.

13.questionText: A filter is labeled N95. What does the 'N' in the designation mean?

14.questionText: Which elements are required in a written respiratory protection program under 29 CFR 1910.134?

options.text: Selection procedures, medical evaluations, fit testing, training, and maintenance

15.questionText: A worker using a half-mask respirator begins to feel short of breath and dizzy. What should they do?

options.text: Breathe more slowly and wait for the symptoms to pass
Remove the respirator while still inside the work area
Exit the work area safely and report the condition to a supervisor
